rewrites.6F390256: The conservative case, 1,822,634 arrivals in 2035, holds existing air access with no added frequencies or routes and continues trade and marketing, with growth in the mature markets and current corridors. Objectives 5 and 7 hold that base. The base case adds 353,144 arrivals to reach 2,175,778. It assumes Wesgro's trade and marketing continue at 2025 intensity while Emirates, Qatar, Ethiopian and Turkish Airlines add frequency and capacity. India, China and regional Africa grow through hub connections. Objectives 1 to 7, 9 and 10 hold it. The accelerated case adds a further 340,504 to reach 2,516,282. It needs direct India and China routes secured and dedicated activation in India, China, the USA and the GCC, with India, China and the Middle East growing ahead of their source markets [[QUERY Q6: Gulf, Middle East or GCC?]]. Objectives 4, 7, 16 and 19 deliver it on top of the base.[^412]
rewrites.16F59856: **Conversion comes first.** Interest far exceeds visits: about 97 million interested travellers against about 1.4 million arrivals. Six barriers hold conversion back and objectives 1 to 4, 7, 9 and 19 answer them (Table 3.2). The work runs all year and in every market. Most of it needs no new seat.[^413]
rewrites.791B8829: **Seats pace growth at the peak.** Airlines have extended capacity past the growth model's 1.8 million seat marker. The 2.5 million target needs about 3.1 million inbound seats (section 2.4). Relief at Cape Town International arrives about 2032 for the international terminal and about 2033 for the runway (section 2.4). Until then, peak growth comes from larger aircraft and added frequency on the full routes and from hub-carrier capacity (objectives 5, 6 and 7). Domestic connections can also grow through George, whose terminal doubles by 2028 or 2029.[^414]
rewrites.304394E4: **If the seat work slips, growth flattens.** The conservative case, with no new seats, ends at 1.82 million in 2035. Projected growth cannot be realised without added capacity or frequency. Without confirmed routes the accelerated case reverts to base. On the full routes, demand work alone cannot close the gap, because carriers are expected to raise fares before they add seats. On the hub routes and in the green season, which have seats to spare, it can.[^415]
